results.title: Plunging GPU prices threaten AI hosts, and new hedges step in
highlights:
## Quick Take

1. 01 Luxor and CME are developing derivatives tied to AI compute prices.
2. 02 These contracts could help GPU owners protect revenue when rental rates fall.
3. 03 Thin liquidity and weak benchmarks could leave operators underhedged.

Companies building AI applications can rent powerful computers instead of buying the equipment themselves, paying for access to the graphics processing units, or GPUs, that run their software.

Lower rental prices make those applications cheaper to operate, but they can also make life harder for the company that bought the machines and needs the rent to pay its debts.

If you've financed a room full of GPUs assuming customers will pay a certain hourly rate, a cheaper competitor can upset the calculation long before you've paid off the equipment. Your machines might still work perfectly, and demand for AI might still be strong, but the amount you earn from each hour could start falling below what the business needs.

Financial contracts could let you protect part of that income by arranging a payment when rental prices fall, in exchange for taking on your own obligations. That's the basic idea behind AI compute derivatives, which let businesses trade their exposure to computing prices separately from renting the computers themselves.

results.title: Cheap GPUs Are Great News, Unless You Financed Them | Whale Factor
highlights:
GPU rental rates have fallen hard, squeezing the AI hosting companies that borrowed billions against their chip fleets. A new set of hedges is emerging to manage the pain, and lenders finally have a reason to care.

What happens when the machines you financed earn less each month than the debt you used to buy them?

...

## The numbers tell the story

Spot rental rates for Nvidia's H100 have fallen to roughly $2 to $3 an hour. A year ago the same chip cleared $8 in tight markets. Some brokers now quote under $2 for long-term reserved capacity.

Meanwhile the debt stacked against those chips keeps growing. CoreWeave has taken on more than $7 billion in financing, much of it underwritten with the GPUs themselves as collateral. Other neoclouds have followed with smaller versions of the same trade.

Do the math. If a host borrowed assuming $6 an hour and now collects $2.50, the interest doesn't care. The gap isn't measured in basis points. It's measured in whether the loan gets refinanced.

...

This is a classic capital cycle, and it's playing out faster than most people expected. High rents in 2023 pulled in enormous supply. New chips shipped. New data centers came online. Supply caught demand, and price did what price always does.

Depreciation is the other half of it. Nvidia talks about four to six year useful life. Anyone who lived through the last two generations will tell you it's closer to two or three when the software keeps moving. On the risk side, that's the whole ballgame for a lender.

results.title: GPU Rental Prices Are Going Up. The Token Price Is Not. - Tech Thought Leaders
highlights:
Executive Summary

Rented GPU capacity is getting more expensive while the price of a token keeps falling. Nebius will raise on-demand rates for the H100, H200, B200 and B300 from 1 October, its second increase in three months, with the B300 up 21 percent to $9.50 a GPU hour. The memory tier moved further still, and Genoa memory rose about 41 percent.

The finding is that the floor under inference pricing is set by memory and power, not by the age of the silicon. Gartner still expects roughly a 90 percent fall in cost per token by 2030, and both things are true at once, because the tokens a GPU hour can produce climb faster than the rent does. Watch the spread between the two numbers. Either one read on its own will mislead you.

The cheapest way to buy AI compute is not getting cheaper. From 1 October, Nebius raises the on-demand rate for four Nvidia accelerators, and it is the second rise in three months. The number most teams track, cost per token, is still heading down.

Both of those live in the same market, which is why the gap between them is the story. If you rent GPU capacity this quarter, a higher GPU hour moves the break-even point for building a feature on your own hardware instead of paying per token to somebody else.

...

Nebius published the change on its own pricing page. The H100 moves from $3.85 to $4.50 an hour, up 17 percent. The H200 rises 20 percent to $5.40. The B200 rises 19 percent to $8.50. The B300 takes the steepest step, up 21 percent to $9.50.

Add the three months since the previous change, and the B300 rate is up roughly 56 percent. The increases were not limited to accelerators. Nebius lifted the AMD EPYC Genoa vCPU rate 25 percent and the Genoa memory rate about 41 percent.

Trackers saw the pressure earlier. SemiAnalysis recorded H100 one-year contract prices climbing from about $1.70 a GPU hour in October 2025 to $2.35 by March 2026, close to 40 percent.

...

Here is the mechanism. The newer the chip, the more high-bandwidth memory it carries, and memory has been the tightest part of the build, as memory market trackers keep recording. The Genoa memory rate rose about 41 percent in the same change, which is the memory squeeze showing up on the bill.

That is also why an aging H100 went up rather than down. The constraint is not how fast the chip is. It is how much memory ships with it, and how much power the rack can push through it.

Per-token prices keep falling while the rented GPU hour climbs. Nebius raises four accelerator tiers on 1 October.

...

The falling number is real too. Gartner expects cost per token to fall roughly 90 percent by 2030. That forecast is about throughput per dollar, not about rent. Serving stacks such as vLLM keep raising what a single GPU hour produces, through paged attention, speculative decoding and prefix caching.

So the rent rises and the token price falls, because the machine does more work in the hour it is rented. Our earlier look at the inference price war and cache economics covers the throughput side.

The specialist clouds are pricing to that scarcity. CoreWeave has been lifting contracted power, from 3.1 gigawatts at the end of 2025 to 4.2 gigawatts by August, and JPMorgan moved its rating to Overweight on stronger compute pricing. Nebius reported second-quarter revenue of $582.3 million, with AI cloud revenue up 514 percent to $574.9 million.

results.title: Would Luxury AI Pricing Encourage a Market for Secondhand Compute Capacity? - AI Tech Model
highlights:
Yes. Luxury AI pricing already encourages a market for secondhand compute capacity.

Secondhand compute capacity means rented spare GPU time from cloud leftovers, peer hosts, or resold hardware. OpenAI sells three ChatGPT Pro tiers at $100, $200 and $500 per month, with Pro 500 providing the highest included usage and exclusive Astra Ultrafast speed, according to OpenAI in its current Pro tiers page. That top-tier cost gives heavy users a clear reason to look for cheaper capacity elsewhere.

...

Amazon EC2 Spot Instances sell spare cloud capacity at up to 90% off On-Demand prices, but AWS can reclaim instances with a two-minute warning, according to AWS in its Spot Instances page. Buyers accept interruption in exchange for very low prices. Peer-to-peer GPU marketplaces work the same way with privately owned cards. Vast.ai listed H100 rentals from about $1.49 per GPU-hour versus up to $6.98 at hyperscalers, and RTX 4090 at about $0.29 versus about $2.79 on AWS, according to CloudZero in its August 2026 GPU price comparison.

The discount is large because the host is monetizing idle hardware. Both models recycle capacity that would otherwise sit unused. Cloud providers fill empty servers. Independent owners rent gaming or mining cards between jobs.

...

Some H100 owners resold surplus GPUs or reduced orders and rented cloud capacity instead once supply constraints eased, according to TechSpot reporting The Information. Short-term rentals made ownership less necessary for variable workloads. Hardware economics support resale. Data-center GPUs usually remain physically sound past economic usefulness, according to 

All Data Center Growth: Why the Distinction Matters in Energy Headlines”>Data Center Knowledge. Resale at 10%-20% of original cost can beat paying disposal costs. Demand for rentals is also growing. The GPU rental market was valued at $39.81 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach $334.87 billion by 2033, according to Data Bridge Market Research. LLM training and inference demand plus high-end GPU shortages drive that growth.

results.title: AWS reportedly raises GPU prices while broader rental costs plunge · CRG TIME
highlights:
Amazon Web Services is reportedly planning a 15% price hike for GPU capacity on October 7, even as falling rental prices elsewhere pressure AI hosting providers.

SJ Sanjay Jamod · Editor 2 CryptoSlate· Crypto Briefing

Why it matters The divergence highlights a split market where major cloud providers retain pricing power while smaller, independent GPU hosts face shrinking margins as hardware access democratises.

Amazon Web Services is reportedly planning to increase its graphics processing unit capacity prices by 15% on October 7. According to Crypto Briefing, the price hike could force artificial intelligence firms to reassess their cloud strategies, potentially impacting the pace of innovation and regional deployment decisions.

Conversely, CryptoSlate reports that plunging GPU rental prices are threatening the business models of AI hosting providers. Companies building AI applications frequently rent powerful computers instead of purchasing the hardware themselves. While lower rental rates make these applications cheaper to operate, they make it harder for the hosts that bought the machines to generate sufficient rental income.

To combat the financial strain of falling rental prices, CryptoSlate reports that new financial hedges are stepping in to help hosts manage their risk. The divergence highlights a shifting market where developers benefit from cheaper access to compute, while the companies hosting the physical hardware face shrinking margins.

results.title: H100 Rates Fell, B200 Rates Rose 79%: The Great GPU Price Divergence of 2026 — CheapestGPU
highlights:
A September 25, 2026 SemiAnalysis report puts a number on one of the clearest GPU cloud price trends of 2026: B200 on-demand rental rates climbed 79% over three months to roughly $8.01/GPU-hr, while the H100 rental price slid to $2.65-3.38/GPU-hr over the same window. Compute-adjusted, B200 is now about 21% more expensive per unit of useful compute than H100 - a full reversal from where the two generations sat in June 2026. These are third-party market figures from SemiAnalysis, not CheapestGPU's own listing prices, and they are exactly the kind of headline number that falls apart the moment you compute-adjust it.

...

- B200 (on-demand, per SemiAnalysis) - roughly $8.01/GPU-hr - up 79% over the prior three months
- H100 (on-demand, per SemiAnalysis) - $2.65-3.38/GPU-hr - down over the same window

Translate the two numbers and the ranking flips. In June 2026, H100 was the pricier compute-adjusted buy. Today B200 costs about 21% more per unit of useful compute than H100 - the reversal is the story, not either sticker rate on its own.

## Why Blackwell memory supply flipped the ranking

SemiAnalysis attributes the move to tight HBM3e supply feeding Blackwell-class parts (B200, and the B300 covered in the B300 order-book post). That is reported, not independently verified here - treat the supply-chain mechanics as the report's claim, not a fact CheapestGPU can confirm from its own board.

What is verifiable from the board: B200 ships at 180GB HBM3e, versus H100 at 80GB HBM3. More than double the memory per GPU is also more than double the exposure to an HBM3e shortage - every B200 that ships consumes memory capacity that a supply crunch makes scarcer and pricier, consistent with Blackwell absorbing more of the squeeze than Hopper.

...

Two illustrative scenarios (order-of-magnitude, not measured - no benchmark data backs these numbers):

- Large-context or large-batch inference. If the model or batch needs more than 80GB of working memory, H100 is not an option at any price - you are paying for B200's 180GB HBM3e whether the headline $/hr is up 79% or not. Here, higher HBM bandwidth and capacity can still produce a lower $/token than a cheaper GPU that cannot fit the job at all.
- A model and batch size that fit comfortably in 80GB without saturating memory bandwidth. Here the extra HBM headroom on B200 buys nothing, and the now-cheaper H100 wins outright on $/GPU-hr and $/token.

The rule has not changed even though the prices did: convert to effective cost for the job you actually have, then pick the generation.

results.title: Oracle Just Rented 100,000 AI Chips To Tencent For $1.60 An Hour. Every Data Center Should Be Worried.
highlights:
On Wednesday night the Financial Times reported that Tencent signed a five year lease for roughly 100,000 advanced AI chips sitting in Oracle data centers across Southeast Asia. Price: about $7 billion, with roughly 30% paid up front. 1 

Do the division and the number gets uncomfortable fast. 100,000 chips running every hour for five years is 4.38 billion GPU hours. Spread $7 billion across that and you get $1.60 per GPU hour.

The same week gave us a very different price. The Ornn H100 index settled at $2.71 on September 30, 2 and on October 1 Nebius lifted its on demand H100 rate to $4.50. 3 Two prices for AI compute, almost 3x apart, in the same seven days. I think the gap between them is the most important number in the AI buildout right now. Which side wins decides what happens to every data center built on today’s rental assumptions.

...

Tencent is stretched too, just in a different way. Its core games and ads business still prints cash. Its AI bill is the strain.

Spot says scarcity. The five year price says glut.

Nebius has now raised on demand prices twice in about three months. Its H100 went from $2.95 in May to $4.50 on October 1, and its first capacity auction cleared 15% above its prior peak. 3 Judged by the spot market, compute is scarce.

Tencent’s lease prices something different: five years of compute at a fixed rate. So I ran the question backwards. Start at today’s $2.71 H100 index and ask what yearly decline makes the five year average land at $1.60. The answer is about 21% a year. That’s the price path Oracle and Tencent effectively agreed on, whether either side said it out loud or not.

Prediction markets lean the same way. Polymarket puts about 65% odds on H100 rental prices finishing 2026 below $3, and the Ornn index fell 11.1% in the week to September 30. 9 Nebius raised prices into that drop. Its hikes also only cover on demand capacity, and committed customers already pay up to 35% less. The spot market is tight at the margin. The long end of the curve is pricing in plenty.

Spot is where you see today’s shortage. The five year contract is where you see what the people with the most information expect.

...

At $1.60 the chip pays back its purchase price with about $20,000 left over to cover five years of power, cooling, staff and interest. And that assumes 100% utilization, which nobody hits. That is barely a business. Most neocloud business plans, and most of the private credit lent against GPU fleets, assume something much closer to today’s spot rates holding for years.

...

Put the two deals side by side and the ... Oracle owns chips and rents them out cheap to raise cash. Amazon owns chips and wants to sell them while keeping their use. Both want the computing power. Neither wants to keep holding the hardware.

So why would the biggest cloud on earth sell hardware it says it can’t get enough of? Andy Jassy has said Amazon won’t have enough capacity in 2026 or 2027, and AWS has raised Capacity Block prices on Nvidia GPUs twice this year, about 15% in January and about 20% in July, with another 15% reportedly flagged for October 7. 15 The answer sits in the cash flow statement.

results.title: Would Falling GPU Rental Prices Rescue Frontier AI Margins? - AI Tech Model
highlights:
No. Falling GPU rental prices will not rescue frontier AI margins alone.

Frontier labs are companies training and serving the largest AI models, and margin is the share of revenue left after compute costs. Cheaper hourly rates help, but total inference bills are growing faster and long-term contracts delay savings. Readers should expect lower cloud bills in places, not restored lab profits.

...

According to AInvest's September 2026 analysis, H100 rentals fell from over $7.00 per GPU-hour in early 2024 to a cohort median around $3.30-$3.40 by mid-2026 CoreWeave GPU rental analysis. The same analysis puts one rental index down about 23% from September 2024 to mid-2025. The IntuitionLabs 2026 pricing guide reports average H100 cloud rates around $3.11 in early 2026, with spot as low as $1.25, as Blackwell B200/B300 supply grew.

The FastGPU September 2026 survey of 28 clouds found the cheapest H100 on-demand listing at $1.79 versus $5.38 at Google Cloud. Crypto Briefing on neocloud Q2 2026 results says specialist GPU instances typically cost 60-70% less than equivalent AWS, Azure and Google Cloud offerings. AInvest market analysis in August 2026 ties this shift to supply moving from acute shortage in 2023 to functional balance in 2026.

...

Sacra's 2026 company profile puts OpenAI gross margin at about 33% in 2025, down from about 40% in 2024, as inference costs reached $8.4 billion Sacra OpenAI profile. It projects inference costs at $14.1 billion in 2026. Reuters review of Anthropic's IPO prospectus reports nearly $4.6 billion in 2025 revenue, up 12-fold, with an $8-plus billion operating loss Reuters IPO prospectus review.

It also reports a $42 billion net loss including about $34 billion in financing-related charges. Lower hourly prices cannot offset many more hours. Larger models, longer answers, and heavier daily use push total compute higher. Unit savings leak away when volume rises faster.

...

Flexible buyers gain first, especially enterprises willing to use specialists. The FastGPU gap of $1.79 versus $5.38 for H100s shows why shopping across clouds matters. The cheapest quote often requires spot capacity or stricter terms. Hosts keep less of the benefit.

AInvest says compressing scarcity premiums removed the pricing power neoclouds enjoyed during the shortage. Cheaper access for users means tougher competition among sellers. Hyperscalers still charge far more for on-demand certainty. The FastGPU survey found cheapest H200 at $2.60 versus $7.91 at AWS, about a 3x gap. Buyers pay extra for brand, region coverage, and guaranteed capacity.

...

Reuters reporting on September 17, 2026 notes Anthropic disclosed $518 billion in future cloud and compute obligations Reuters Nebius price report. Falling spot rentals do not immediately cut those committed costs. Price moves are also uneven.

The same Reuters report notes Nebius raised selected Nvidia on-demand rentals 17%-21% effective Oct. 1, 2026. Median declines can hide increases on popular configurations. Treat the $1.79 low quote as a best case, not a budget for reserved capacity.

results.title: Renting GPU Compute in 2026: Why There Are Now Three Prices for the Same GPU (And How to Avoid Overpaying) - AI LLM News | Independent AI & LLM Coverage
highlights:
Ask ten people what it costs to rent an H100 and you will get ten answers. Most of them are right. Published on-demand rates for the same chip currently run from roughly $1.38 per GPU-hour on marketplaces to $12.29 on Azure, and that 12x spread comes from one May 2026 market survey.

Renting GPU compute used to be a simple trade: pay by the hour, skip the $30,000 card. In 2026 the market is more complicated. Spot prices have softened while one-year contract prices have climbed. A tradable futures market for GPU rental is about to appear. Anyone who rents on the old assumption that “GPU prices only fall” can lose real money.

...

### The 2026 Twist: Three Prices for One GPU

Most guides quote a single “H100 price.” That hides the most useful fact about the market right now.

1. Spot and marketplace prices stayed low. The cheapest on-demand and spot offers for an H100 sit around $1.25 to $3 per hour. Spheron’s October 2026 pricing comparison lists H100 at $2.65 on-demand and $2.21 on spot.

2. Committed contracts got more expensive. SemiAnalysis’s H100 rental index shows one-year contract pricing rising almost 40%, from $1.70 per GPU-hour in October 2025 to $2.35 by March 2026. Capacity coming online was largely pre-booked.

3. Newer chips cost more, and the gap moves. Silicon Data’s index data put the H200 premium over the H100 at 5.8% in May 2026 and 12.1% in July, peaking at 16.2%.

A low spot price therefore does not mean abundant capacity. If you plan a long project and wait for prices to fall, you may pay more later. If you only need burst capacity, the spot market is usually the cheaper route.

### Typical GPU Rental Prices (Mid-to-Late 2026)

Prices change often, so treat these as ranges and check the provider’s page before you commit.

| Provider type | Example | H100 per GPU-hour (approx.) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Marketplace | Vast.ai | ~$1.4–$2.0 |
| Specialist cloud | RunPod, Lambda, Crusoe, Nebius | ~$2.7–$4.0 |
| Specialist (8-GPU node) | CoreWeave | ~$6.16 per GPU |
| Hyperscaler | AWS p5.48xlarge ($55.04/hr for 8 GPUs) | ~$6.88 |
| Hyperscaler | Azure ND96isr H100 v5 ($98.32/hr for 8 GPUs) | ~$12.29 |

Sources: IntuitionLabs’ provider comparison and Spheron’s July 2026 H100 survey.

...

### Hidden Costs That Change the Bill

The hourly rate is only part of what you pay.

Data egress. Hyperscalers charge for data leaving their network. At the commonly cited $0.09 per GB, moving 5 TB out costs about $450. RunPod’s documentation states there are no ingress or egress fees on Pods.

Storage that bills while the GPU is off. On RunPod, a stopped volume disk costs $0.20 per GB per month, double the running rate. For a 200GB volume that is $40 a month instead of $20, and a standard network volume would cost about $14.

Minimum bundles. CoreWeave’s H100 pricing is per 8-GPU node, so you cannot rent one GPU. You pay for all eight.

Interruptions. Spot capacity can be reclaimed. AWS gives a two-minute interruption warning, and that is the maximum you should assume anywhere.

Idle time. This is the largest hidden cost of all. A GPU left running overnight costs the same as one training a model.

...

### Something New: GPU Rental Is Becoming a Financial Market

CME Group and Silicon Data have announced two compute futures contracts, covering the H100 and the B200, targeted for October 5, 2026, pending regulatory review. Each contract represents one month of rental for the chip and settles against Silicon Data’s published index. Per a Spheron analysis of the launch, settlement is in cash, not hardware.

For a small team this will not change much immediately. It does mean GPU prices will soon have a public reference curve, and it gives a hyperscaler or large lab a way to lock in costs. It may also make the opaque pricing described above easier to read.
